summary:
Saskatchewan stands under the national framework of Canada. Provincial human rights law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, and transgender people are able to change their legal gender in the province under its own rules.

The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent before students under 16 may use a gender-related preferred name or have their gender identity recognised at school. The province passed the Act while invoking the notwithstanding clause of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which shields the provision for five years from being struck down on Charter grounds.

On 22 August 2023 the Saskatchewan education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies requiring schools to seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, requiring parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and pausing third-party school programs. Human rights groups called for repeal of the law, and litigation followed.

UR Pride Centre challenged the policy. The Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan ruled on 11 August 2025 in Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74, setting aside the 2023 chambers decision and holding that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where section 33 has been invoked, so the policy stands. The same judgment granted the government's appeal in part and held that a judge does have jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, allowing UR Pride's litigation to continue in the Court of King's Bench.

On 6 November 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it would hear the appeals brought by both the province and UR Pride against that Court of Appeal decision. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

The consent requirement governs school settings and binds school-age residents of Saskatchewan. It imposes no document, entry or screening condition on visitors, but it is the clearest expression in the province of official hostility toward trans recognition.

No Saskatchewan-specific rule or case governing the placement of transgender prisoners in provincial correctional institutions appears in the sources; provincial correctional policies vary and only national policy for federal custody is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International Canada participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the 11 August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada, arguing that use of the notwithstanding clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The organisation's position is that courts may still determine whether the province's pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the clause shields the law from being struck down.

The province argued that its use of the override should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada, acting as co-counsel, said UR Pride would continue the litigation and noted that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years, a period the courts did not disturb.

Both sides asked the Supreme Court of Canada to expedite the hearing alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21, placing Saskatchewan's school policy among the live override disputes before the national court.

Saskatchewan is one of three provinces, with British Columbia and Ontario, that grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing a wider range of queer and trans families than most other Canadian jurisdictions permit.
localsOnly:
Under the parental inclusion and consent policies announced on 22 August 2023, Saskatchewan schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused.

Saskatchewan legalised same-sex adoption in 2001, and the province grants parental status to three or more intentional parents, which supports a wider range of trans and queer family formations than most provinces allow.

Residents challenging the consent rule must proceed through the Court of King's Bench after the Court of Appeal held that the override shields the policy from being struck down but does not remove the courts' power to declare whether it limits Charter rights. Human rights groups continue to call for repeal.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources describe the 11 August 2025 appeal ruling differently. One states that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 Charter breaches where section 33 was invoked, so the policy stands. The other states that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights and that the litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. Both are reported as the same judgment; the precise scope of the holding is unresolved in the sources.

The constitutional question remains open. The Supreme Court of Canada accepted the appeals on 6 November 2025 and no merits ruling has yet been issued, so the current status of the consent rule is that it is in force and shielded while under review.

Correctional policy for transgender prisoners is documented only at the national level, for federally operated institutions. No Saskatchewan statute, institutional rule or case on placement, housing or care of trans prisoners in provincial institutions is sourced, and provincial correctional policies are noted as varying without being specified for this province.

The sources contain no Saskatchewan-specific data on anti-trans violence or hate crime broken out by gender identity, and do not address access to gender-affirming care, provincial identity-document processing, or facility access within the province. Those questions are not sourced rather than settled.
